synthesis: Choosing longer Riemann–Siegel blocks reduces the number of outer blocks but turns each block into a polynomial-phase query of higher degree or wider coefficient range. The complete reduction is useful only when truncation error, direct remainders, per-query work, and reusable preprocessing all fit the same global exponent; in the cubic case, recursive shortening increases the cubic coefficient until a boundary solver or a final precomputed transform must absorb the resulting representation complexity.
source_support: Unit u07 derives the block-size trade and tabulates how fewer blocks entail higher phase degree and broader coefficients. Unit u10 carries that trade through amplitude and phase truncation, global error accounting, and the two K-regimes that keep cubic preprocessing at the 4/13 target. Unit u14 explains why recursion shortens length while increasing the cubic coefficient and why the terminal high-degree case costs about the fourth power of its final length.
nonparaphrase_operation: Composes a local block representation tradeoff, a global error-and-budget contract, and recursive stopping logic into a resource conservation principle: sequence-length savings are real only when the harder query family is amortized within the saved outer work.
limits: The source proves the advertised transfer only for its normalized quadratic and restricted small-cubic interfaces and their stated preprocessing budgets. It does not show that arbitrary larger cubic coefficients or independently varying higher-degree phases remain affordable; the outline explicitly says their required precomputations become too costly, and several exact exponent formulas are representation-sensitive.
quality_reason: Accepted because three distinct sections jointly establish the causal chain from block scale to query complexity to budget-compatible dispatch and terminal preprocessing; no one parent alone supplies that full mechanism.

synthesis: Repeated Poisson or van der Corput transformation contracts an exponential sum only when an intervening normalization prevents inversion back to the original representation and the transformed phase remains in a reusable family. Quadratic phases have exact Gaussian closure, whereas cubic phases recover only approximate closure by using coefficient smallness to retain the quadratic and cubic terms and expand higher terms and amplitude corrections into controlled weights and error.
source_support: Unit u06 explicitly identifies normalization between Poisson applications as the reason repetition does not return to the starting sum. Unit u12 shows that Gaussian self-similarity preserves quadratic form, normalization of b bounds the new length by roughly half, and no-saddle remainders remain a separate computational obligation. Unit u13 locates the cubic obstruction in the square-root saddle phase and, under bK≥1 and |cK²|≤0.01b, expands the nonclosing terms to obtain shorter weighted cubic sums plus error and a no-saddle remainder.
nonparaphrase_operation: Contrasts exact and approximate closure to isolate three jointly necessary ingredients for iteration—normalization, contraction, and controlled treatment of everything outside the closed phase family—rather than treating transformation alone as progress.
limits: The cubic reduction is confined to the quantitative smallness and normalization hypotheses stated in u13; outside them the same-type recursion is not justified. In this outline the no-saddle cubic remainder is expected to be cheaper and the displayed recurrence is only suggested before later proof, so neither may be silently treated as discharged by these parent units.
quality_reason: Accepted because the parents jointly explain why normalization creates progress, why quadratic iteration closes exactly, and how cubic smallness repairs the loss of closure while preserving explicit proof and remainder burdens.

synthesis: Saddle reduction produces bounded-degree polynomial-phase sums whose degree rises when the terminal length is small relative to the inherited scale. Independent-coordinate FFT gridding is affordable while that degree is uniformly bounded, but in the high-degree short-length regime the higher coefficients must instead be kept in their shared analytic parameterization: expressing them through τ, ρ, and γ turns a growing coefficient vector into a six-variable interpolation problem and restores the preprocessing budget.
source_support: Unit u16 converts the central saddle contribution into weighted polynomial-phase sums, chooses the truncation degree from log N/log M, and bounds the higher coefficients. Unit u17 shows that for R/9≤n≤R the degree is at most 12, so dyadic translation and independent-coordinate FFT gridding cost at most the target fourth-power budget. Unit u18 treats n<R/9, where the degree grows and independent gridding is costly, derives β_{s+3}=τη_s(ρ,γ), and uses six-variable Cauchy interpolation and FFT counts to bound total preprocessing by O(Λ⁵K^{4μ}).
nonparaphrase_operation: Uses the moderate-regime construction as a counterfactual baseline, identifies exactly why it fails at higher degree, and preserves the analytic generator of the coefficients to replace ambient coefficient dimension with intrinsic parameter dimension.
limits: The compression depends on the particular saddle-derived identities, bounds, and inherited admissibility conditions for τ, ρ, and γ; numerical smallness or correlation by itself does not imply the same grid reduction. Exact contour setup, grid spacings, derivative constants, and source formulas remain representation-sensitive.
quality_reason: Accepted because three distinct units establish the production of the high-degree phases, the bounded-degree regime where naive gridding works, and the dependency-aware replacement needed when it does not; the resulting relation is a concrete refinement unavailable from any single parent.
